messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing a psychological case vignette
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

Write a realistic clinical case vignette for a patient with PTSD.
The vignette should read as a cohesive, flowing portrait — not a structured report.
Weave together who this person is, what happened to them, how they experience their
symptoms day to day, how they cope, and what toll this takes on their life and relationships.


Do not use section headers, numbered points, or clinical labels for symptoms.
Write 200–300 words in third person.
Cover: presenting complaints, trauma background, cognitive distortions, avoidance, and maintaining factors.
Avoid excessive jargon - write for a clinical case conference audience.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient presenting with PTSD.
Patient demographics:
- Age: 74
- Gender: Male
- Ethnicity: North American
- Relationship Status: Widowed
- Occupation: Combat Pilot
- Trauma Type: Physical abuse by romantic partner
- Pcl5: 56

# The Weight of Coming Home

Raymond is a 74-year-old widowed man who spent the better part of three decades as a combat pilot, logging thousands of hours over hostile terrain, making split-second decisions that determined whether he and his crew came home alive. He is accustomed to danger. He knows how to compartmentalize, how to stay calm when everything around him is falling apart. What he was never prepared for was the danger that waited for him inside his own home.

His second marriage began well enough. He had been lonely after retiring from active duty, and Margaret came into his life with warmth and humor. Within two years, however, something shifted. The first time she struck him, he told himself it was an aberration — she had been drinking, she was under stress. He said nothing. He had survived anti-aircraft fire. He was not going to be undone by a domestic argument. That reasoning, he now understands, kept him in the house for another four years.

The violence escalated gradually, the way most things do when you are too close to see the pattern. There were objects thrown, bruises he covered with long sleeves, a broken rib he attributed to a fall when his physician asked. Raymond could not find language for what was happening to him. Men who flew combat missions did not get hurt by their wives. The shame of that belief held him in place far longer than the fear did.

The marriage ended when Margaret struck him across the face with a glass bottle during an argument in the kitchen. He required stitches. A neighbor had called the police. Standing in the emergency room that night, Raymond felt something inside him go very quiet in a way that has never entirely come back.

That was six years ago. He lives alone now in a small house in a mid-sized city, and on the surface his days appear orderly. He tends a garden. He reads military history. He attends a weekly breakfast with a group of fellow veterans. But the nights are a different matter entirely. He sleeps for no more than three or four hours before waking in a cold sweat, heart hammering, certain that someone is in the room with him. He checks the locks two, sometimes three times before he can settle again — if he settles at all. He keeps the bedroom light on.

During the day, unexpected sounds — a cabinet slamming, glass breaking on a television program — send a jolt through his body that takes long minutes to subside. He finds himself scanning rooms when he enters them, noting exits, positioning himself with his back to the wall in restaurants. These are habits he recognizes from his flying days, repurposed now for a threat he can no longer see clearly. He does not fully understand why his nervous system has decided that the kitchen is the most dangerous room in his house, but he eats most of his meals standing at the counter, rarely sitting at the table.

He has become quieter with the men at his breakfast group, pulling back from conversations that drift toward relationships or family. He told one of them, once, in the vaguest of terms, that his marriage had been difficult. The man nodded and changed the subject, and Raymond felt both relieved and profoundly alone. He carries a persistent low-grade belief that something is wrong with him — not with what was done to him, but with him, for having allowed it, for not having stopped it sooner, for being a man who flew into combat and could not protect himself at his own kitchen table.

He presents as composed, measured, and quietly watchful. He chooses his words carefully, as if each one requires clearance before it can be spoken. When he describes the night with the bottle, his voice remains level, but his hands, resting on his knees, press down hard against his legs, as though he is holding something in place that might otherwise come loose.
